body.en: A recursive method calls itself. Every correct recursive method has a base case, which is answered directly without a further call, and a recursive case, which calls the method on a smaller problem that moves towards the base case. fact(n) = 1 if n <= 1 (base case), else n * fact(n − 1) (recursive case). Without a reachable base case the calls never end and the program fails with a StackOverflowError.

title.en: The call stack, and recursion versus iteration

body.en: Each call gets its own *stack* frame holding its parameters, local variables and the place to return to. Frames are pushed as calls are made and popped as they return, so the last call made is the first to finish (LIFO). Recursion often gives shorter, clearer code for problems defined in terms of themselves (factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, tree traversal, Tower of Hanoi), but it uses more memory and time for the calls. Iteration (loops) uses a fixed amount of memory. Any recursive method can be rewritten iteratively.

tagline.en: What a recursive method is, why it needs a base case, how the call stack winds and unwinds, and how to trace a recursive method's output step by step.

myth.en: A base case is optional: the method will stop on its own when n becomes small.

truth.en: Without a reachable base case the method calls itself for ever, until the call stack runs out of memory and Java throws a StackOverflowError. In a loop, a wrong condition just repeats; it feels as if recursion should also "run out". But each new call needs more stack space, and n keeps going down past 0 into negative numbers, so nothing stops it except the error.

say.en: A recursive method calls itself; it needs a base case and a recursive case that shrinks the problem.
Each call has its own activation record on the call stack.
Winding: calls pile up. Unwinding: they return in reverse order.
Statements before the call run in calling order; statements after it run in reverse order.
Missing or unreachable base case → StackOverflowError.
